title: How the Torah is read
hook: a handwritten scroll, read aloud on Shabbat, Mondays and Thursdays

segments.voice: Yesterday, shavua: the camp of practices closed, and you chose three to keep. Your line was the week has a shape. Today a new camp opens: the text, one portion a week.

Most books are printed by a machine, thousands of copies at once. This one never is. Every letter is written by hand, with a quill, in ink, on parchment, by a trained scribe, one letter at a time. It's rolled on two wooden poles, dressed in a cloth cover, and kept in a cabinet at the front of the synagogue. When it comes out, people stand. Some reach out to touch it with the fringe of a prayer shawl, then kiss the fringe. And then someone reads it out loud, in a chant handed down from teacher to student.
screen: `EVERY LETTER BY HAND.` → `ROLLED ON TWO WOODEN POLES.` → `WHEN IT COMES OUT, PEOPLE STAND.`

segments.voice: Sefer Torah means a book of Torah: the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written by a sofer, a scribe, on sheets of parchment sewn together. The rules are exacting. Every letter must be formed correctly, and a single missing or broken letter can make the scroll unfit until it's fixed. There are no vowels in it and no punctuation, so the reader learns ahead of time how the words sound. The reader doesn't touch the parchment with a finger, but follows the line with a yad, a small pointer, often shaped like a hand. And it's chanted aloud in a set melody, with marks passed down for each word. When? On Shabbat morning, a full weekly portion. On Monday and Thursday mornings, and Shabbat afternoon, a shorter piece. Why Monday and Thursday? The Talmud connects it to the Israelites in the wilderness, who went three days without water and grew weak. The sages compared Torah to water, and arranged the readings so that three days never pass without it. Public reading appears in the Bible itself. In the book of Nehemiah, Ezra the scribe stands on a wooden platform and reads the Torah aloud to the whole people, men, women and all who could understand, and teachers explain it so everyone follows. That's the heart of it. In the synagogue, Torah isn't read silently in a corner. It's heard, together, out loud, with the whole room listening.
screen: `SEFER TORAH: A HANDWRITTEN SCROLL.` · `NO VOWELS, A POINTER CALLED A YAD.` · `SHABBAT, MONDAYS AND THURSDAYS.` · `EZRA READS IT TO EVERYONE.` · then, large: `HEARD, NOT JUST READ.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and for this minute read nothing: just listen to the sounds around you, near and far. Then remember a voice that once read to you, a parent at bedtime, a teacher, anyone, and hear the words the way you heard them then.
Sefer Torah. A book of Torah: a handwritten scroll of the five books of Moses, read aloud to everyone.
Your line: heard, not just read. A scroll is made for a listening room. Day one hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: In synagogues the Torah scroll is taken from the ark and chanted aloud on Shabbat morning and afternoon and on Monday and Thursday mornings, as well as on festivals; the reader follows the text with a pointer called a yad.
